e.etymology: From Old English Mildthryth, joining milde, 'gentle', and thryth, 'strength', the name of an Anglo-Saxon abbess and saint. Revived by the Victorians, it was the sixth most popular US girls' name in the 1910s.
namesakes: Mildred Pierce (title character of the novel and Joan Crawford film)
Mildred Loving (plaintiff in Loving v. Virginia)
Mildred Ratched (Nurse Ratched of One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest)

e.etymology: From Greek Basileios, 'royal, kingly', from basileus, 'king'; Saint Basil the Great was a 4th-century bishop. The herb's name has the same root. Arabic Basil, 'brave', is a separate name with the same spelling.
namesakes: Basil Rathbone (actor, the classic screen Sherlock Holmes)
Basil Fawlty (John Cleese's hotelier in Fawlty Towers)
e.note: Spelled like the herb. Americans say the herb BAY-zul; the name is traditionally BAZ-ul.

e.etymology: A feminine spelling of Casey, from the Irish surname O Cathasaigh, 'descendant of Cathasach', a byname meaning 'vigilant'.
A spelling of Mekhi, the name made familiar by actor Mekhi Phifer of ER and 8 Mile. Its source is not documented; it sounds like Malachi without the middle syllable.
From Arabic nahla, 'a drink of water, a first sip'. A near-identical Arabic word with a different h means 'honeybee'. Halle Berry chose the name for her daughter in 2008, which lifted it in the US.
e.note: Sounds the same as Nala, the lioness in The Lion King.

e.etymology: A short form of names ending in -gina, such as Regina, Georgina and Italian Luigina. Italian film star Gina Lollobrigida, born Luigia, made it fashionable in the 1950s.
namesakes: Gina Lollobrigida (Italian film star)
Gina Rodriguez (actress, Jane the Virgin)
Gina Gershon (actress)

e.etymology: The older English spelling of Anthony, from the Roman family name Antonius, whose origin is unknown. The h was added in the 1500s from a mistaken link to Greek anthos, 'flower'.
namesakes: Mark Antony (Roman general, ally of Caesar and lover of Cleopatra)
Antony Blinken (US Secretary of State, 2021 to 2025)

e.etymology: Either Desiree written without its accents, French for 'desired', from Latin desiderare, or the English word itself, a Puritan virtue name: Desire Minter sailed on the Mayflower.
e.note: Read as the plain English word it suggests longing or lust; many families say it dez-ih-RAY, like Desiree.

e.etymology: From the giant redwood trees of California. The genus Sequoia was named in 1847, by most accounts in honor of Sequoyah, the Cherokee scholar who created the Cherokee writing system.

assoc.t: giant sequoia, the largest tree on Earth
Sequoia Capital, Silicon Valley venture capital firm

e.etymology: A phonetic respelling of Dakota, the name of the Dakota people of the northern plains, which means 'friends, allies' in their language and was given to two US states.

assoc.t: North Dakota and South Dakota (same sound)

e.etymology: A Portuguese and Spanish spelling of French Amaury, from the Germanic name Amalric, joining amal, 'work, vigor', and ric, 'ruler'. Two crusader kings of Jerusalem were named Amalric.

A Spanish name; alita is also the Spanish word for 'little wing'. US use rose after the 2019 film Alita: Battle Angel, based on a Japanese manga whose heroine was renamed Alita for the English edition.

assoc.t: Alita, cyborg heroine of Alita: Battle Angel

e.etymology: From Latin amare, 'to love', and deus, 'god': one who loves God, or is loved by God. It is the Latin equivalent of Greek Theophilus, Mozart's baptismal name, and the 1984 film Amadeus fixed the link to him.
namesakes: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (composer)

assoc.t: Rock Me Amadeus, 1985 Falco pop hit

e.etymology: The Basque form of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, 'who is like God?'. In the United States it has also been used as a phonetic spelling of Michael.
A modern name that jumped in the US after Mission: Impossible 2 (2000), whose heroine is Nyah Nordoff-Hall. It is sometimes treated as a form of Nia, Swahili for 'purpose'.
The Portuguese and Galician form of Catherine, from Greek Aikaterine, the name of Saint Catherine of Alexandria. Its original meaning is unknown; early Christians tied it to Greek katharos, 'pure'.
A modern Hindi name popularly explained as 'first ray of the sun'. It is probably related to Sanskrit arusha, 'reddish, the sun', a Rigveda word for the red horses of the fire god Agni.
A modern name in the family of Myla, Kayla and Layla, built on May. The similar Finnish name Maila began as a nursery form of Maria.
A respelling of Kyson, a modern American name made by adding -son to Ky, in the pattern of Tyson and Bryson.
From Italian donna, 'lady, woman', from Latin domina, 'mistress of the house'. English speakers coined it as a given name in the 19th century, and it was later also taken as a feminine of Donald.
namesakes: Donna Summer (disco singer)
Donna Karan (fashion designer)
Donna Reed (actress, It's a Wonderful Life)

e.etymology: An English spelling of Irish Sile, the Irish form of Cecilia, from the Roman family name Caecilius, based on caecus, 'blind'. It was most popular in the mid-20th century.
namesakes: Sheila E. (percussionist and singer)
Sheila Jackson Lee (Texas congresswoman)

assoc.t: sheila, Australian slang for a woman

e.note: In Australia 'sheila' is casual slang for any woman.

e.etymology: From the Welsh surname Lloyd, from llwyd, 'grey', a nickname for a grey-haired man. English speakers who could not manage the Welsh ll also turned it into Floyd.
namesakes: Lloyd Bridges (actor)
Lloyd Christmas (Jim Carrey's character in Dumb and Dumber)
Lloyd Austin (US Secretary of Defense, 2021 to 2025)

assoc.t: Lloyd's of London, the insurance market
Lloyd, the green ninja in LEGO Ninjago

e.etymology: The Portuguese form of Paul, from the Roman family name Paulus, 'small, humble', spread by the apostle Paul. In Spanish it is a less common alternative to Pablo.
namesakes: Paulo Coelho (Brazilian author of The Alchemist)

e.etymology: From Greek Hermione, derived from Hermes, the messenger god. In myth she is the daughter of Helen and Menelaus; Shakespeare gave the name to the queen in The Winter's Tale. It is unrelated to German Hermine.
namesakes: Hermione Granger (Harry Potter's brilliant friend)
Hermione (the wronged queen in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale)

assoc.t: Hermione Granger of the Harry Potter series

e.etymology: A recent name without a settled origin. It follows the sound of Alana and Aylin and the -lana ending of Hawaiian-style names such as Kailana.
A very recent name with no documented source. It resembles the Basque name Naiara and the Armenian name Nairi.

From Hebrew Hiram, probably Phoenician in origin and a short form of Ahiram, 'my brother is exalted'. Hiram, king of Tyre, sent cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's Temple. Puritans brought the name to America.
namesakes: Hiram Revels (first Black US senator)
Hiram Bingham (explorer who brought Machu Picchu to world notice)
Hiram Lodge (Veronica's father in Riverdale)

e.etymology: A spelling of Marley, an English surname from places named with Old English leah, 'woodland clearing', after a word for 'pleasant', 'boundary' or 'marten'. Marli is also a separate Brazilian name.
A modern American name in the pattern of Jabari, Kamari and Amari. It has no documented meaning of its own.

A respelling of the surname Coe, an old English nickname from a word for the jackdaw. Its recent rise follows Texas country singer Koe Wetzel, whose parents named him for outlaw country singer David Allan Coe.
namesakes: Koe Wetzel (country rock singer)

e.etymology: A spelling of Kelsey, an English surname from the Old English personal name Ceolsige, joining ceol, 'ship', and sige, 'victory'. Kelsey became a popular girls' name in the 1980s and 90s.
The Italian form of Latin Vitus, linked to vita, 'life'. Saint Vitus, a boy martyr from Sicily, made it a favorite in southern Italy, and immigrants carried it to America in the early 1900s.
namesakes: Vito Corleone (the Godfather, played by Marlon Brando and Robert De Niro)
e.note: Closely tied to Vito Corleone of The Godfather and to mob-movie stereotypes.
